rounding_convention: decimal.Decimal throughout; rates/monthly amounts at full precision, every JE and schedule amount rounded to whole dollars with ROUND_HALF_UP applied once per period. Schedules closed to EXACTLY zero by plugging the final period with the remaining unamortized balance (the $11,200 defense layer runs $862 + 6 x $1,723 + final plug $1,722 = $11,200).

journal_entries.memo: Item 1 - purchase copyright, finite 12-yr useful life
Item 2 - purchase franchise, indefinite life (no amortization)
Item 3 - purchase patent, 7-yr useful life (< 14-yr legal life)
Item 4 - external counsel fees to register trade name, indefinite life
Item 5 - internal development costs expensed as incurred (not capitalized)

journal_entries.memo: Item 7 - successful defense of purchased patent capitalized to Patent
Item 8 - two-year municipal license, finite 2-yr life
Year-1 amortization: finite-life intangibles only (franchise, trade name, goodwill not amortized)

notes: Classification: finite-life = copyright ($72,000/12yr), patent ($56,000/7yr useful < 14yr legal), capitalized patent-defense costs ($11,200), 2-year license ($24,000/2yr); indefinite-life (not goodwill) = franchise $110,000 and registered trade name $8,400; goodwill = $1,250,000 - $980,000 = $270,000; expense = $145,000 internal R&D. Item 7: successful defense is capitalized to the patent, classification unchanged (still finite-life), amortized prospectively over the 78 months of useful life remaining at July 1 -> $11,200 x 6/78 = $861.54 -> $862 in Year 1. Year-1 amortization = 6,000 copyright + 8,000 patent + 862 defense + 12,000 license = $26,862; franchise, trade name and goodwill are not amortized (impairment tested). Dec 31 Yr 1 carrying amounts: patent $58,338 (67,200 - 8,862), copyright $66,000, franchise $110,000, trade name $8,400, license $12,000, goodwill $270,000; total $524,738. If an instructor instead amortizes the defense layer over a full 7 years (11,200/7 x 1/2 = $800) Year-1 amortization would be $26,800 and the patent $58,400 - that convention does not fully amortize the layer by the end of the patent's useful life, so the remaining-life (78-month) basis is used here.
